en: And Tootoru gained the power of speech.
Tootoru plunged into the tumult;
For those who understand, strife is a great affliction.
Tootoru entered the uproar,
When reined aside, he seemed to fly;
Tootoru climbed the ridge.
To foolish, empty-headed Kyyaz
Tootoru began confiding his secret.
Folding back his ears like a kulan,
Sweeping the earth like a whirlwind,
Making the ground crumble under his tread,
Drawing in his belly beneath Kyyaz,
Rearing and pitching forward,
The great bay horse swayed and plunged,
Straining as though about to fly,
Neighing and bucking,
The beast spoke words to Kyyaz—
To Kyyaz of the Jediger
He spoke as follows:
“Hero Kyyaz, valiant one,
I was your swift steed Tootoru.
We were joined when you were no bigger than a louse,
We came together when you were the size of a thumb,
We met when you were tiny as a tick.
You were a child at play,
And I a foal just beginning to graze.
I became a noble warhorse,
And anyone seeking me was a stranger.
You became khan over the waters of Jeti-Özön,
Yet you rage and will not listen.
Go into the earth, Kyyaz—farewell;
You shall never again ride upon my neck!
You shall no longer charge raging at the foe,
Nor roam Jeti-Özön again!”
Thus Tootoru spoke these words,
Tootoru the horse speaking like a man,
And saying this—
Aichürök, daughter of the peri,
Thought, “Should Kyyaz hear this speech,
He might suddenly start a quarrel.”
Such was Chürök’s nature:
Whoever saw her fame was startled,
For she had learned wondrous spells.
Eighty charms and a thousand incantations—
She had memorized and recited them all.
She had no equal in sorcery,
That radiant infidel;
Her cunning surpassed all, and she was most knowing.
Behind the sorceress
Hung a tassel from her hair;
Within that very tassel
Was a dangling yellow key,
A key that opened every single thing.
Many were her graces—
If only you could see poor Chürök!
Thinking, “If the horse speaks, he will hear it,
And the peerless hero Kyyaz
May suddenly start a quarrel;
If he learns of it, he will raise a dispute,
And mighty-armed Kyyaz,
Shouting and starting a brawl,
May tear my collar apart;
Yet if I ignore it, that too will be wrong,”
With matchless quickness
She seized and swung
The beaded tassel bound to her hair,
And with a resounding crack
Struck Tootoru on the forehead.
You care about nothing,
You swaggering Kyyaz.
You let a woman take your horse—
That is what you have become, Kyyaz.
Bloodily afflicted, you grieved;
May witless Kyyaz come to ruin—
You have lost the horse Tootoru!
Your wing is broken at your side;
You are undone, brave Kyyaz!
Parted from your swift steed,
Disaster has overtaken you, Kyyaz!
Jagged cliffs and a severed road—
Alas, Kyyaz, farewell!
Suffer misery and come to grief—
Alas, Kyyaz, farewell!
This woman will take you as her spoil,
Gouge out your eyes,
Strip the brows from above them,
And though she now caresses you,
In the end she will cut off your head!
She will dig your grave deep
And show your eyes a marvel.
Though you plead, she will not heed your words;
Like water poured on fire, she will quench
Your breath, brave Kyyaz!
Though you plead, she will not heed your words;
She will fold your body double while you live,
And, fawning slave Kyyaz,
This woman will cut short your breath.
You heed no word spoken,
You follow no road shown,
You stubborn Kyyaz.
Hero Kyyaz, brave gray wolf,
Your wings have been clipped;
You have lost Tootoru,
The steed you cherished!
The renowned steed’s tail
Was once braided five strands at a time;
Would a lionhearted warrior
Ever give his horse to a woman?
Speech was his custom.
He was a renowned steed,
And of ordeals six months away
Tootoru would speak like a man
And give warning.
If there was a net none could escape,
A calamity no living soul could cross,
An army encircling the land
From which no winged creature could flee,
Whenever he was mounted for battle,
Tootoru, my winged steed,
Was accustomed to speak of it.
The reason he could speak was this:
This very horse Tootoru
Had appeared by providence
From the desert of Mediyan,
From the pass of It-Kyyan,
Where no cawing crow was found,
No croaking raven flew,
There was no grass for beasts to chew,
No water for man to swallow—
From the desert no dog could cross,
From the shore where no living thing roamed.
He was encountered as a two-year-old
And found as a three-year-old.
He was raised in a dark place,
With an amulet fastened to his head;
The blood-drinking brass-beaked crone
Tested him there and approved him.
No other soul could ride him,
And he could not refrain from speaking.
“Hold and turn my horse’s mouth;
What will Tootoru say now?
Wait, woman Chürök, stand still!
No human speaks such words—
What is my beast, my bay, saying?”
Thus spoke brave Kyyaz,
Now raging, now calming,
A sheathless sword strapped to him;
Blood-stained Kyyaz raged.
When the key struck his forehead,
Tootoru, being a swift steed,
Staggered in circles,
Swaying like one dazed,
Yet did not topple and fall;
He shied away, then recovered.
The bay horse that had been speaking
Lost the use of his tongue.
His forelock fell over his eyes;
The hair tassel split his forehead
A full span wide.
Subdued by the blow,
The poor bay horse
Had his speaking tongue bound.
Alas, that woman Aichürök
Raised her stately head like a banner,
Turned a woman’s head into a warrior’s,
And struck the speaking steed
Down level with the black earth;
She deafened his hearing ears
And bound his tongue.
Brave Kyyaz of the Jediger
Was that day in Jeti-Özön,
In the pleasure garden of the fortress,
Seated there
Upon his throne, ruling the people.
Such was Kyyaz when you saw him,
His bluish fist as large as a knob;
Such was his appearance.
He raged like a blue-maned lion,
As insight came to him from the unseen;
He roared in anger,
Calling out to Aichürök,
His bellow splitting heads,
His shout splitting stones:
“Accursed Chürök, wait there!
If he speaks, that is my learning;
Tootoru is my wing.
When grave trouble befalls an honored man,
When a black day weighs upon his soul,
Though you came to us as a captive slave,
You have shown your valor.
Like a ravine untouched by wind,
You have proved yourself a mountain pass.
You have shown yourself a lion
Who could subdue the peoples of the world.
If you are a hero, if you are a lion,
Your terror is like a club-sized fist.
You charged and shouted,
Calling out, ‘Aichürök!’
If you are mighty, if you are a lion,
If you truly are hero Kyyaz,
Would you behave like this?
Why do you shout so?
Shall I go deliberately to the village,
Saying, ‘My lord, has the world ever seen the like?’
If you would slaughter me, here is my head;
If a woman has committed a crime,
First make your horse speak.”
So Aichürök spoke,
Seized the reins of the plunging Tootoru,
And turned his head;
With these words your Chürök
Stood speaking to Kyyaz.
For all the ages until now,
Peerless Kyyaz, you have done wrong;
Time and again,
You have scorned us as slave women.
The sable cap upon your head—
Who has not worn one tilted proudly?
While fortune crowns his head,
Who has not gone about roaring?
At the sight of a champion,
How many enemies have not panicked?
I was that same Chürök,
But captivity brought my head to shame;
Among us, holy Kyyaz held supreme power.
Hero, we are slaves in your hands,
The bare ground where horses are tethered,
Wretches fallen into captivity.
Seized by bloodthirsty fury,
Unable to make the black earth crack
Beneath the weight of Kyyaz’s wrath,
He flailed about in anger,
Saying, “What did the horse say?”
Brave Kyyaz of the Jediger
Came running in a swagger.
Aichürök, Akun’s daughter,
Spoke these words:
“If your horse speaks, heed his tongue,
By your father’s grave, brave Kyyaz!
You refuse to grant the horse’s strength
To your lawfully wedded wife—
What a fool you are, Kyyaz!
Forty carpets from the winding pass—
I know the nature of this horse.
Let us pass before him
And hear him speak, since you claim
To be a holy man.
Make your horse speak, brave Kyyaz;
Though we are women, let us hear.
Can one who merely tends livestock and keeps a household
Be a hero such as you?
Is it right to call a wretch like you
A hero?
Hero, you have braced your black Zulfiqar sword
Against your side
As though an enemy had come to grapple with you.
